claim: The thermal limits of C. elegans are 12°C and 25°C, defined as temperatures where >90% of embryos hatched.
source: We thus found that the thermal limits of C. elegans were of 12°C and 25°C (Figure 1A)
evidence: Based on progeny tests showing embryonic viability at different temperatures, with operational definition of thermal limits as edges of temperature range with >90% hatching.

claim: The thermal limits of C. briggsae are 14°C and 27°C, defined as temperatures where >90% of embryos hatched.
source: those of C. briggsae of 14°C and 27°C (Figure 1B)
evidence: Based on progeny tests showing embryonic viability at different temperatures.

claim: C. briggsae usually lives in warmer climates than C. elegans.
source: in line with the fact that C. briggsae usually lives in warmer climates than C. elegans (Prasad et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Prasad et al., 2011.

claim: The thermal range defined by upper and lower limits ensures robust propagation of the population.
source: The thermal range defined by these upper and lower limits ensures robust propagation of the population
evidence: Inference from the operational definition of thermal limits at 90% viability threshold.

claim: The thermal range is narrower than the reproductive range for C. elegans (9°C–26°C).
source: is narrower than merely the reproductive range for C. elegans (9°C–26°C [Anderson et al., 2011])
evidence: Comparison with cited reproductive range from Anderson et al., 2011.

claim: The thermal range is narrower than the reproductive range for C. briggsae (14°C–30°C).
source: or C. briggsae (14°C–30°C [Anderson et al., 2007; Prasad et al., 2011])
evidence: Comparison with cited reproductive range from Anderson et al., 2007 and Prasad et al., 2011.

claim: The vast majority of monitored cellular features were temperature-dependent within the thermal range.
source: Our analysis established that the vast majority of the monitored features were temperature-dependent within the thermal range (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Based on quantification of 35 cellular features across temperatures within thermal range.

claim: The fraction of time spent in mitosis exhibited temperature-independent behavior within the thermal range.
source: some features, including the fraction of time spent in mitosis (Figure 2B) and cell division asymmetry (Figure 2C), exhibited a temperature-independent behavior
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of cellular features showing no correlation with temperature.

claim: Cell division asymmetry exhibited temperature-independent behavior within the thermal range.
source: some features, including the fraction of time spent in mitosis (Figure 2B) and cell division asymmetry (Figure 2C), exhibited a temperature-independent behavior
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis showing constant asymmetry within thermal range.

claim: Temperature-compensation mechanisms are at play for some cellular features.
source: suggesting that temperature-compensation mechanisms are also at play
evidence: Inferred from observation that some features remain constant despite temperature changes.

claim: The duration of mitosis decreased monotonically with increasing temperatures within the thermal range in C. elegans.
source: Thus, the duration of mitosis, which decreased monotonically with increasing temperatures within the thermal range, plateaued beyond both lower and upper thermal limits in C. elegans (Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on time-lapse microscopy measurements of cell cycle duration at different temperatures.

claim: The duration of mitosis plateaued beyond both lower and upper thermal limits in C. elegans.
source: Thus, the duration of mitosis, which decreased monotonically with increasing temperatures within the thermal range, plateaued beyond both lower and upper thermal limits in C. elegans (Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on time-lapse microscopy measurements showing deviation from monotonic decrease at thermal limits.

claim: Cell cycle duration was not faster in C. briggsae than in C. elegans at any temperature.
source: we found that cell cycle duration was not faster in C. briggsae than in C. elegans at any temperature (Figure 3A, compare with Figure 2A)
evidence: Based on comparison of cell cycle duration measurements between the two species.

claim: Cell cycle duration within the thermal range was well described by Arrhenius kinetics in C. elegans with 92% of explained variance.
source: Interestingly, cell cycle duration within the thermal range was well described by Arrhenius kinetics in C. elegans (92% of explained variance; 'Materials and methods') (Arrhenius, 1915).
evidence: Based on fitting cell cycle duration data to Arrhenius model.

claim: In C. briggsae, data beyond 25°C reduced the explained variance of Arrhenius fit from 86% to 39%.
source: In C. briggsae, by contrast, the data beyond 25°C reduced the explained variance from 86% to 39%
evidence: Based on Arrhenius model fitting to C. briggsae cell cycle duration data.

claim: Cell cycle duration plateaued already below the upper thermal limit in C. briggsae.
source: suggesting that cell cycle duration plateaued already below the upper thermal limit in this species
evidence: Inferred from poor fit of Arrhenius model when including data beyond 25°C.

claim: Mitosis duration is a limit-sensitive feature.
source: underscoring the fact that mitosis duration is a limit-sensitive feature
evidence: Inferred from observation that mitosis duration behavior changes at thermal limits in both species.

claim: The asymmetry of the first cell division in C. elegans was constant within the thermal range.
source: We also observed that the asymmetry of the first cell division in C. elegans, which was constant within the thermal range, decreased below 12°C (F-test p = 0.0005) and increased above 25°C (F-test p < 10−7) (Figure 2C; see 'Materials and methods' for statistics).
evidence: Based on quantification of daughter cell sizes at different temperatures.

claim: The asymmetry of the first cell division in C. elegans decreased below 12°C (F-test p = 0.0005).
source: We also observed that the asymmetry of the first cell division in C. elegans, which was constant within the thermal range, decreased below 12°C (F-test p = 0.0005) and increased above 25°C (F-test p < 10−7) (Figure 2C; see 'Materials and methods' for statistics).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of daughter cell size measurements.

claim: The asymmetry of the first cell division in C. elegans increased above 25°C (F-test p < 10−7).
source: We also observed that the asymmetry of the first cell division in C. elegans, which was constant within the thermal range, decreased below 12°C (F-test p = 0.0005) and increased above 25°C (F-test p < 10−7) (Figure 2C; see 'Materials and methods' for statistics).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of daughter cell size measurements.

claim: The asymmetry of the first cell division in C. briggsae increased beyond the upper thermal limit at both 28°C and 29°C (F-test p-value < 10−10).
source: In C. briggsae, the asymmetry of the first cell division also increased beyond the upper thermal limit, at both 28°C and 29°C (F-test p-value < 10−10) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of daughter cell size measurements in C. briggsae.

claim: A reciprocal decrease in asymmetry was not observed at the lower thermal limit in C. briggsae.
source: However, a reciprocal decrease was not observed at the lower thermal limit in this species
evidence: Based on analysis of cell division asymmetry data at lower temperatures.

claim: Spindle pole oscillations are weaker in C. briggsae than in C. elegans.
source: perhaps because spindle pole oscillations are weaker in C. briggsae than in C. elegans (Riche et al., 2013) (compare panel D in Figures 2, 3)
evidence: Supported by citation to Riche et al., 2013 and comparison of data in figures.

claim: Weaker spindle pole oscillations potentially limit the dynamic range over which asymmetry can be tuned in C. briggsae.
source: potentially limiting the dynamic range over which asymmetry can be tuned
evidence: Speculative inference about mechanism explaining lack of asymmetry decrease at lower limit.

claim: Embryo size was larger at the lower end of the thermal range (12°C for C. elegans).
source: Thus, embryo size was larger at the lower end of the thermal range (i.e., 12°C for C. elegans, Figure 2E; 14°C for C. briggsae, Figure 3E)
evidence: Based on measurements of embryo area at different temperatures.

claim: Embryo size was larger at the lower end of the thermal range (14°C for C. briggsae).
source: Thus, embryo size was larger at the lower end of the thermal range (i.e., 12°C for C. elegans, Figure 2E; 14°C for C. briggsae, Figure 3E)
evidence: Based on measurements of embryo area at different temperatures.

claim: Embryo size tended to decrease with increasing temperature within the thermal range.
source: and tended to decrease with increasing temperature within the thermal range
evidence: Based on trend analysis of embryo size measurements across temperatures.

claim: The decrease in embryo size with increasing temperature is in line with the 'temperature-size rule' observed in the vast majority of ectotherms.
source: This is in line with the 'temperature-size rule' observed in the vast majority of ectotherms (Atkinson, 1994; Forster et al., 2012)
evidence: Comparison with established pattern in literature supported by citations.

claim: The temperature-size relationship is in agreement with previously reported data for C. elegans at 10°C vs 20°C.
source: and in agreement with previously reported data for C. elegans at 10°C vs 20°C (Van Voorhies, 1996)
evidence: Supported by citation to Van Voorhies, 1996.

claim: Below the lower thermal limit, embryo size was significantly reduced in C. elegans (F-test p < 10−7).
source: Strikingly, below the lower thermal limit, embryo size was actually significantly reduced in both C. elegans and C. briggsae (Figures 2E, 3E; F-test p < 10−7 and p = 0.001, respectively).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of embryo size measurements.

claim: Below the lower thermal limit, embryo size was significantly reduced in C. briggsae (F-test p = 0.001).
source: Strikingly, below the lower thermal limit, embryo size was actually significantly reduced in both C. elegans and C. briggsae (Figures 2E, 3E; F-test p < 10−7 and p = 0.001, respectively).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of embryo size measurements.

claim: A reversal of the temperature size rule below the lower thermal limit has been reported in protists and in Drosophila.
source: Such a reversal of the temperature size rule below the lower thermal limit has also been reported in protists and in Drosophila (Karan et al., 1998; Atkinson et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Karan et al., 1998 and Atkinson et al., 2003.

claim: The size decrease below the lower thermal limit may reflect cold-inhibited mitochondrial function according to the MASROS hypothesis.
source: These observations are compatible with the MASROS hypothesis, which posits that such a size decrease below the lower thermal limit may reflect cold-inhibited mitochondrial function (Atkinson et al., 2006).
evidence: Interpretation based on MASROS hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: Beyond the upper thermal limit, a plateau in embryo size was observed in both C. elegans and C. briggsae.
source: Beyond the upper thermal limit, we observed a plateau in the size of both C. elegans and C. briggsae embryos (Figures 2E–3E).
evidence: Based on embryo size measurements at temperatures above upper thermal limit.

claim: Embryos in both C. elegans and C. briggsae were more elongated beyond the upper thermal limit (C. elegans F-test p = 0.0004, C. briggsae F-test p < 10−10).
source: Interestingly, however, we observed that embryos in both species were more elongated beyond the upper thermal limit (Figures 2F–3F; F-test p = 0.0004 and F-test p < 10−10, respectively).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of embryo shape (length/width ratio) measurements.

claim: Embryo elongation results in an increase of the surface area, thus potentially augmenting its availability for oxygen diffusion.
source: Such an elongation results in an increase of the surface area, thus potentially augmenting its availability for oxygen diffusion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Geometric inference about surface area increase from elongation.

claim: Changes in cell size and shape are signature hallmarks of the thermal limits.
source: Overall, these results reveal that changes in cell size and shape are signature hallmarks of the thermal limits.
evidence: Summary inference from observed changes in size and shape at thermal limits.

claim: Respiration increased exponentially within the thermal range in wild-type C. elegans embryos.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, we found that respiration increased exponentially within the thermal range, as predicted by Arrhenius-like kinetics (Arrhenius, 1915).
evidence: Based on oxygen consumption measurements at different temperatures.

claim: Respiration departed from Arrhenius-like kinetics below the lower thermal limit (F-test p-value < 10−4).
source: Strikingly in addition, this analysis uncovered that respiration departed from Arrhenius-like kinetics both below the lower thermal limit (F-test p-value < 10−4) and above the upper thermal limit (F-test p-value < 10−10), in support of reduced respiration at those temperatures (Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of oxygen consumption measurements.

claim: Respiration departed from Arrhenius-like kinetics above the upper thermal limit (F-test p-value < 10−10).
source: Strikingly in addition, this analysis uncovered that respiration departed from Arrhenius-like kinetics both below the lower thermal limit (F-test p-value < 10−4) and above the upper thermal limit (F-test p-value < 10−10), in support of reduced respiration at those temperatures (Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of oxygen consumption measurements.

claim: There is a clear correlation between relative reduction in aerobic capacity beyond thermal limits and increased lethality at those limits.
source: Although we do not know whether the observed relative reduction in aerobic capacity beyond both thermal limits as compared to within the thermal range contributes to increased lethality at those limits, our results show a clear correlation between these features.
evidence: Inference from observed correlation between respiration and viability data.

claim: Embryonic lethality was reduced towards the lower thermal limit in atp-2(RNAi) compared to within the thermal range.
source: Importantly, in addition, this analysis uncovered that embryonic lethality was reduced towards the lower thermal limit as compared to within the thermal range in all three cases, as well as towards the upper thermal limit in both cyc-1(RNAi) and nuo-1(RNAi) (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Based on progeny tests with RNAi-treated embryos at different temperatures.

claim: Embryonic lethality was reduced towards the lower thermal limit in cyc-1(RNAi) compared to within the thermal range.
source: Importantly, in addition, this analysis uncovered that embryonic lethality was reduced towards the lower thermal limit as compared to within the thermal range in all three cases, as well as towards the upper thermal limit in both cyc-1(RNAi) and nuo-1(RNAi) (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Based on progeny tests with RNAi-treated embryos at different temperatures.

claim: Embryonic lethality was reduced towards the lower thermal limit in nuo-1(RNAi) compared to within the thermal range.
source: Importantly, in addition, this analysis uncovered that embryonic lethality was reduced towards the lower thermal limit as compared to within the thermal range in all three cases, as well as towards the upper thermal limit in both cyc-1(RNAi) and nuo-1(RNAi) (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Based on progeny tests with RNAi-treated embryos at different temperatures.

claim: Embryonic lethality was reduced towards the upper thermal limit in cyc-1(RNAi) compared to within the thermal range.
source: Importantly, in addition, this analysis uncovered that embryonic lethality was reduced towards the lower thermal limit as compared to within the thermal range in all three cases, as well as towards the upper thermal limit in both cyc-1(RNAi) and nuo-1(RNAi) (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Based on progeny tests with RNAi-treated embryos at different temperatures.

claim: Embryonic lethality was reduced towards the upper thermal limit in nuo-1(RNAi) compared to within the thermal range.
source: Importantly, in addition, this analysis uncovered that embryonic lethality was reduced towards the lower thermal limit as compared to within the thermal range in all three cases, as well as towards the upper thermal limit in both cyc-1(RNAi) and nuo-1(RNAi) (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Based on progeny tests with RNAi-treated embryos at different temperatures.

claim: The capacity of the mitochondrial respiratory chain is restricted beyond both thermal limits.
source: These results offer strong experimental support to the notion that the capacity of the mitochondrial respiratory chain is restricted beyond both thermal limits
evidence: Inference from reduced lethality of respiratory chain RNAi at thermal limits.

claim: Other metabolic routes may be used to a larger relative extent at thermal limits in the face of reduced respiration.
source: and raise the possibility that other metabolic routes are used to a larger relative extent at those temperatures in the face of reduced respiration
evidence: Speculative inference from reduced impact of respiratory chain compromise at limits.

claim: Embryo size was not significantly affected upon RNAi-mediated depletion of atp-2.
source: Interestingly, we found that whereas embryo size was not significantly affected upon RNAi-mediated depletion of atp-2 (Figure 4E)
evidence: Based on embryo size measurements in atp-2(RNAi) embryos.

claim: atp-2(RNAi) embryos were more elongated at both 12°C (U-test p = 0.0034) and 16°C (U-test p = 0.0039).
source: these embryos were more elongated at both 12°C and 16°C (Figure 4F, U-test p(12°C) = 0.0034, p(16°C) = 0.0039)
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of embryo shape measurements in atp-2(RNAi).

claim: In nuo-1(RNAi), embryo size was significantly reduced at both 12°C (U-test p = 0.02) and 16°C (U-test p < 10−3).
source: In nuo-1(RNAi), embryo size was significantly reduced at both temperatures (U-test p(12°C) = 0.02, U-test p(16°C) < 10−3, Figure 4E)
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of embryo size measurements in nuo-1(RNAi).

claim: In cyc-1(RNAi), embryo size was significantly reduced at 12°C (U-test p < 10−3).
source: whereas a similar response was observed in cyc-1(RNAi) embryos at 12°C (U-test p(12°C) < 10−3, Figure 4E)
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of embryo size measurements in cyc-1(RNAi).

claim: Depletion of three respiratory chain components shares the net result of increasing surface to volume ratio within the thermal range.
source: While it remains to be investigated why the cellular consequences of depleting these three components differ to some extent, remarkably, they share the net result of increasing surface to volume ratio within the thermal range, thus mimicking the situation in the wild-type beyond the thermal limits.
evidence: Inference from combined effects of size and shape changes in RNAi conditions.

claim: The cellular hallmarks observed at the thermal limits of wild-type embryos reflect restricted aerobic capacity.
source: Therefore, these results strongly support the notion that the uncovered cellular hallmarks observed at the thermal limits of wild-type embryos reflect restricted aerobic capacity.
evidence: Inference from recapitulation of thermal limit phenotypes by respiratory chain compromise.

claim: The thermal response of select cellular features changed precisely at the limit temperatures defined by embryonic viability tests.
source: Interestingly, we uncovered that the thermal response of select cellular features changed precisely at the limit temperatures defined by embryonic viability tests (see Figure 1A–B).
evidence: Based on comparison of cellular feature changes with viability-defined thermal limits.

claim: A mere 10% decrease in embryonic viability is associated with readily observable cellular changes during the first cell cycle.
source: While we do not know whether these cellular hallmarks are responsible for the observed increased lethality beyond the thermal limits, we note that a mere 10% decrease in embryonic viability is associated with readily observable cellular changes during the first cell cycle.
evidence: Observation from correlation between viability threshold and cellular phenotypes.

claim: Aerobic metabolism plays a smaller relative role towards the thermal limits than within the thermal range.
source: Importantly, experiments in which mitochondrial respiration is compromised revealed that aerobic metabolism plays a smaller relative role towards the thermal limits than within the thermal range
evidence: Inference from reduced lethality of respiratory chain RNAi at thermal limits.

claim: Other metabolic routes may be favored to produce energy at thermal limits.
source: raising the possibility that other metabolic routes are favored to produce energy
evidence: Speculative inference from reduced reliance on aerobic metabolism at limits.

claim: Changes in size and shape observed beyond the thermal limits in wild-type can be recapitulated within the thermal range by impairing aerobic metabolism.
source: Furthermore, these experiments uncover that the changes in size and shape observed beyond the thermal limits in the wild-type can be recapitulated within the thermal range by impairing aerobic metabolism
evidence: Based on observations in respiratory chain RNAi experiments.

claim: Changes in size and shape arise in response to restricted aerobic metabolism.
source: strongly supporting the view that these changes arise in response to restricted aerobic metabolism
evidence: Inference from recapitulation of phenotypes by respiratory chain compromise.

claim: Restricted aerobic metabolism is a general principle characterizing thermal limits in multicellular organisms in water and on land.
source: Together, our work provides critical experimental evidence supporting the notion that restricted aerobic metabolism is a general principle characterizing thermal limits in multicellular organisms in water and on land.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental findings in C. elegans and C. briggsae.

claim: Cold-induced increase in unsaturated fatty acids in cyanobacteria and Arabidopsis contributes to setting the lower thermal limit.
source: Thus, cold-induced increase in unsaturated fatty acids in cyanobacteria, Arabidopsis (Hazel, 1995) and C. elegans contributes to setting the lower thermal limit (Svensk et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hazel, 1995 and Svensk et al., 2013.

claim: Cold-induced increase in unsaturated fatty acids in C. elegans contributes to setting the lower thermal limit.
source: Thus, cold-induced increase in unsaturated fatty acids in cyanobacteria, Arabidopsis (Hazel, 1995) and C. elegans contributes to setting the lower thermal limit (Svensk et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Svensk et al., 2013.

claim: Unsaturated fatty acid changes only account for 16% of the observed difference in cold tolerance at 10°C vs 25°C in C. elegans.
source: although it only accounts for 16% of the observed difference in cold tolerance at 10°C vs 25°C in C. elegans (Murray et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Murray et al., 2007.

claim: Warm-induced increase in post-translational glycosylation contributes to setting the upper thermal limit in Drosophila melanogaster, Danio rerio and C. elegans.
source: Moreover, warm-induced increase in post-translational glycosylation also contributes to setting the upper thermal limit in Drosophila melanogaster, Danio rerio and C. elegans (Radermacher et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Radermacher et al., 2014.

claim: Defects in synaptonemal complex assembly contribute to setting the upper organismal limit in C. elegans.
source: In addition, defects in synaptonemal complex assembly (Bilgir et al., 2013) and in sperm (Harvey and Viney, 2007) contribute to setting the upper organismal limit in C. elegans.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bilgir et al., 2013.

claim: Defects in sperm contribute to setting the upper organismal limit in C. elegans.
source: In addition, defects in synaptonemal complex assembly (Bilgir et al., 2013) and in sperm (Harvey and Viney, 2007) contribute to setting the upper organismal limit in C. elegans.
evidence: Supported by citation to Harvey and Viney, 2007.

claim: Restricted aerobic metabolism is an important piece of the puzzle that contributes to defining both thermal limits.
source: The restricted aerobic metabolism experimentally uncovered here is another important piece of the puzzle that contributes to defining both thermal limits.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental findings in context of other known mechanisms.

claim: A mismatch between oxygen supply and demand has been suggested to play a role in setting thermal limits in multicellular organisms.
source: A mismatch between oxygen supply and demand has been suggested to play a role in setting thermal limits in multicellular organisms.
evidence: Statement of hypothesis from literature.

claim: The OCLTT hypothesis derives in part from the observation that oxygen partial pressure in aquatic organisms is constant within a given thermal range and decreases both below the lower thermal limit and above the upper thermal limit.
source: This hypothesis, referred to as the oxygen- and capacity-limited thermal tolerance (OCLTT), derives in part from the observation that oxygen partial pressure in aquatic organisms is constant within a given thermal range and decreases both below the lower thermal limit and above the upper thermal limit (Pörtner, 2002; Pörtner et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pörtner, 2002 and Pörtner et al., 2006.

claim: The metabolic status of some aquatic organisms has been shown to peak at a given temperature and to decrease both below and above that.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, the metabolic status of some aquatic organisms has been shown to peak at a given temperature and to decrease both below and above that (Melzner et al., 2006; Wittmann et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Melzner et al., 2006 and Wittmann et al., 2008.

claim: Tolerance to high temperatures is increased in an amphibian crab when the animal is in the air compared to when it is in water, reflecting the reduced cost of oxygen supply in air.
source: Interestingly too, tolerance to high temperatures is increased in an amphibian crab when the animal is in the air compared to when it is in water, reflecting the reduced cost of oxygen supply in air (Giomi et al., 2014), again supporting the OCLTT hypothesis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Giomi et al., 2014.

claim: Thermal limits in complex organisms are characterized by a mismatch in oxygen supply and demand, which would result in reduced energy production and thus limit reproduction and growth.
source: Overall, these data suggest that thermal limits in complex organisms are characterized by a mismatch in oxygen supply and demand, which would result in reduced energy production and thus limit reproduction and growth (Pörtner, 2002; Pörtner et al., 2006).
evidence: Inference from cited literature on OCLTT hypothesis.

claim: The temperature-dependence of oxygen diffusion is significantly lower than that of metabolism.
source: Intriguingly, the temperature-dependence of oxygen diffusion is significantly lower than that of metabolism (Woods, 1999)
evidence: Supported by citation to Woods, 1999.

claim: Body size decreases with augmented temperature in the vast majority of ectotherms ('temperature-size rule').
source: One possible solution is suggested by the observation that body size decreases with augmented temperature in the vast majority of ectotherms ('temperature-size rule') (Atkinson, 1994; Forster et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Atkinson, 1994 and Forster et al., 2012.

claim: The slope of the 'temperature-size rule' is steeper for aquatic organisms than terrestrial organisms, in agreement with the lower availability of oxygen in water compared to air.
source: In support of this, the slope of this 'temperature-size rule' is steeper for aquatic organisms than terrestrial organisms, in agreement with the lower availability of oxygen in water compared to air (Forster et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Forster et al., 2012.

claim: Alterations in cell size in response to changes in temperature within the thermal range are adaptive responses to preserve aerobic capacity according to the MASROS hypothesis.
source: This has led to the suggestion that alterations in cell size in response to changes in temperature within the thermal range are adaptive responses to preserve aerobic capacity, which has been dubbed the MASROS hypothesis (Maintain Aerobic Scope—Regulate Oxygen Supply) (Atkinson et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Atkinson et al., 2006.

claim: The MASROS hypothesis predicts that aerobic metabolism, measured as respiration, should decrease beyond both the lower and the upper thermal limit as compared to within the thermal range.
source: Furthermore, the MASROS hypothesis predicts that aerobic metabolism, measured as respiration, should decrease beyond both the lower and the upper thermal limit as compared to within the thermal range, once the organism can no longer compensate for the insufficient oxygen availability.
evidence: Inference from MASROS hypothesis framework.

claim: The central predictions of the MASROS hypothesis have not been challenged experimentally in an integrative fashion.
source: To our knowledge, these central predictions of the MASROS hypothesis have not been challenged experimentally in an integrative fashion.
evidence: Statement about gap in literature.

claim: The extent to which restricted aerobic metabolism is a general principle characterizing thermal limits remains unclear.
source: Therefore, the extent to which restricted aerobic metabolism is a general principle characterizing thermal limits remains unclear.
evidence: Statement about gap in knowledge motivating the study.

claim: Organisms tend to distribute in the ocean and on land according to latitude as well as depth and altitude.
source: Partly as a result, organisms tend to distribute in the ocean and on land according to latitude as well as depth and altitude, although other elements such as availability of food and light also play a role in shaping preferred habitats (Pörtner, 2002; Pörtner et al., 2006; Prasad et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pörtner, 2002; Pörtner et al., 2006; Prasad et al., 2011.

claim: Availability of food and light also play a role in shaping preferred habitats of organisms.
source: although other elements such as availability of food and light also play a role in shaping preferred habitats (Pörtner, 2002; Pörtner et al., 2006; Prasad et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Pörtner, 2002; Pörtner et al., 2006; Prasad et al., 2011.

claim: The mechanisms that set the thermal limits remain incompletely understood.
source: Despite their importance, the mechanisms that set the thermal limits remain incompletely understood.
evidence: Statement about gap in knowledge.

claim: All organisms live within a given thermal range, beyond which growth and fecundity decrease.
source: All organisms live within a given thermal range, beyond which growth and fecundity decrease (Pörtner et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pörtner et al., 2006.

claim: Embryonic respiration was reduced in cyc-1(RNAi) embryos, reaching on average 56% ± 13% of the wild-type levels (t-test p-value < 10−3).
source: We ascertained that embryonic respiration was reduced in cyc-1(RNAi) embryos, reaching on average 56% ± 13% of the wild-type levels under the assay conditions (t-test p-value < 10−3; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Based on oxygen consumption measurements in cyc-1(RNAi) embryos.

claim: All three RNAi conditions (atp-2, cyc-1, nuo-1) were embryonic lethal to some extent.
source: Importantly, we found that all three RNAi conditions were embryonic lethal to some extent (Figure 4B–D), probably owing to decreased energy production through respiration, although we cannot exclude that the observed lethality stems from changes in pH or increased reactive oxygen species.
evidence: Based on progeny tests with RNAi-treated embryos.

claim: The observed lethality in respiratory chain RNAi conditions probably owes to decreased energy production through respiration.
source: probably owing to decreased energy production through respiration, although we cannot exclude that the observed lethality stems from changes in pH or increased reactive oxygen species
evidence: Speculative inference about mechanism of lethality.

claim: The observed lethality in respiratory chain RNAi conditions may stem from changes in pH or increased reactive oxygen species.
source: although we cannot exclude that the observed lethality stems from changes in pH or increased reactive oxygen species
evidence: Alternative speculative explanation for observed lethality.

claim: C. briggsae has been estimated to have diverged from C. elegans 18–100 million years ago.
source: which has been estimated to have diverged from C. elegans 18–100 million years ago (Stein et al., 2003; Cutter, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Stein et al., 2003 and Cutter, 2008.

claim: The variance of cellular features does not increase beyond the thermal limits as compared to within the thermal range.
source: Note that the variance of cellular features does not increase beyond the thermal limits as compared to within the thermal range.
evidence: Observation from statistical analysis of cellular feature measurements.

claim: C. briggsae can develop at warmer temperatures than C. elegans.
source: Moreover, although C. briggsae can develop at warmer temperatures than C. elegans (Figure 1A–B) (Prasad et al., 2011)
evidence: Based on thermal limit data and citation to Prasad et al., 2011.
